title: CAVE: A Structured Credit Assignment Approach for Fragmented Visual Evidence Reasoning
claim: Existing process rewards score whole trajectories or final answers; ours assigns structured credit to each intermediate reasoning action.
layout: 2 stacked panels: (a) four-sample strip, (b) side-by-side pipelines, dotted divider
description: The figure has two stacked panels. Panel (a) is a row of four example tasks, each with an image, a question and an answer. Sample 1 is a grid of shapes in which a 2x2 pattern has to be matched against a larger 4x4 image. Sample 2 is a colored US map comparing the areas of regions. Sample 3 is a multi-line metro map used to check whether a route needs a transfer. Sample 4 is an aerial remote-sensing photo with an upper-right inset. Panel (b) is split by a dotted vertical line. On the left, 'Existing process reward' runs image to VLM to a block of think/zoom/answer actions to a prediction. A single 'Trajectory quality' arrow and an 'Answer' arrow lead into a tall orange reward bar. On the right, CAVE has the same flow, but three arrows (Evidence acquisition, Belief update, Adaptive focus control) leave individual actions and enter the reward. The colors are pastel, with red and pink action blocks.
caption: (a) Samples of Fragmented Visual Reasoning. The examples cover Geometry, Geography, Route, and Remote-Sensing tasks. Samples 1--3 require organizing confusable and subtle evidence across separate regions, while Sample 4 requires matching nonlocal relations in a noisier real image. (b) Comparison between existing process-reward methods and CAVE. Existing methods usually rely on trajectory-level or answer-side optimization, whereas CAVE assigns action-level structured credits according to the reasoning contributions of intermediate visual-evidence reasoning steps.
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general multimodal reasoning, yet remain challenged in integrating nonlocal visual information to support semantically underdetermined visual reasoning. We describe this challenge as Fragmented Visual Reasoning. To this end, we propose Credit Assignment for Visual Evidence (CAVE), a structured process-reward method based on GRPO for interleaved visual reasoning. Specifically, CAVE evaluates the contribution of intermediate steps at the action level via three complementary reasoning process signals: belief update, evidence acquisition, and adaptive focus control, thereby guiding the model to optimize each reasoning action and learn more reliable visual reasoning strategies. Meanwhile, we construct TRACER-Bench, which covers four nonlocal and semantically confusable reasoning dimensions and provides key intermediate evidence to supervise reasoning paths. Experiments demonstrate that CAVE substantially improves performance on tasks requiring fragmented visual evidence integration, covering both public benchmarks and our newly introduced TRACER-Bench, while retaining competitive performance on general multimodal evaluations. Further analyses reveal that CAVE effectively improves the visual reasoning capacity and exhibits stronger robustness under longer-range and deeper cross-region dependencies.
